Former Patriarca crime family soldier Vincent “Gigi” Marino sits down with VladTV to recount his early life in Boston and Revere, his path from aspiring Massachusetts State Trooper to armed robber, and the street decisions that led to decades behind bars. Marino details how discovering the truth about his biological father, Edward Marino, changed his outlook, and how stickups escalated into bank robberies, nightclub jobs, and armored car hits.

In this segment, Marino breaks down an armored truck robbery that erupted into gunfire when a guard pulled his weapon. Though no one was hit, the crew escaped with the wrong bag—filled with change. He also recalls a North End Boston bank robbery near FBI agent John Connolly and Boston Police official Eddie Walsh, a dye-pack disaster, mob pressure, and a smoother $150,000 score using a telephone company truck. Marino also discusses New Hampshire charges, a suppression hearing, and his long prison history.

Prez argues Iran is using negotiations to stall, regroup, and maintain leverage over the Strait of Hormuz, while challenging claims that the U.S. is clearly winning. The conversation turns to Trump’s repeated statements that Iran is “begging” for a deal, with Prez pointing to ongoing attacks, missiles, ships being hit, and the idea that America has supposedly “won” dozens of times already.

recentItems.title: Delta Force Soldier Dale Comstock on Afghanistan Ambush That Made Him Quit Going to War (Part 9)
recentItems.description:
Become a VladStocks Member now: https://www.youtube.com/vladtv/join

Part 8: https://youtu.be/Ygail0zMH5U
Part 1: https://youtu.be/U21AbA_cZII
--------
Retired Delta Force operator Dale Comstock sits down with Vlad to recount the Afghanistan mission that convinced him to end his combat deployments. Moving at night with a 26-vehicle convoy through a Taliban-controlled seven-kilometer stretch, Comstock describes hearing enemy radio traffic as fighters set up IEDs, probing fire, and ambush positions around his team. With wounded to evacuate, an AH-64 Apache helicopter providing emergency close air support, and Taliban fighters adapting their tactics, the convoy was forced to drive directly through the kill zone under heavy suppression fire. Comstock recalls thinking of his wife and three children, deciding that if he survived, he would “hang the guns up.” He also explains how relentless gunfire may have prevented an IED trigger man from detonating charges. A gripping firsthand account of Afghanistan, special operations, convoy warfare, and the human cost of repeated deployments.

recentItems.title: Marine Cody Alford on Seeing His Machine Gunner's Arm Blown Off During Ambush (Part 2)
recentItems.description:

--------
Marine veteran Cody Alford sits down with Vlad to recount a brutal 2004 combat engagement after being shot in the head on his first day in the fight. Alford describes returning to patrols with a damaged helmet, moving into an “empty” house with Echo Company, and coming under a coordinated ambush involving grenades, machine gun fire, snipers, and insurgents firing from nearby rooftops and a minaret. He recalls Zach Cannon protecting a SAW machine gun after suffering catastrophic injuries, Marines wounded by shrapnel, and the helplessness of seeing his best friend Aaron Austin shot while fire superiority had to come first. Alford also discusses Doug Zembiec, Delta Force medics, Gomez Perez, Abrams tanks, Cobra helicopters, a 500-pound JDAM, and the delayed casualty evacuation to Mac K. A firsthand account of close-quarters combat, battlefield trauma, and survival under fire.

recentItems.description:
Become a VladStocks Member now: https://www.youtube.com/vladtv/join
--------
Retired Marine Raider and Scout Sniper Cody Alford sits down with VladTV to recount his path from Texas teen inspired by Tom Berenger’s *Sniper* to an 18-year-old Marine deployed to Iraq after 9/11. Alford describes arriving through Kuwait, staging at Bahari near one of Saddam Hussein’s former palace sites, and being attached to Echo Company during the Battle of Fallujah—one of the Iraq War’s most intense urban fights. He breaks down the role of Marine snipers, the presence of foreign fighters, and how units like the 101st Airborne, Delta Force, and 2/1 Marines operated in the chaos. Alford also details the moment he was shot in the helmet on his first day inside Fallujah, the concussion and out-of-body experience that followed, and how the battle quickly proved far different from training at Camp Pendleton.

The conversation explores the hard questions behind modern warfare: retaliation, civilian casualties, children caught in conflict, and whether violence only creates the next generation of enemies. Part 7: https://youtu.be/pQLfZcRlwAg
Part 1: https://youtu.be/U21AbA_cZII
--------
Former Delta Force operator Dale Comstock sits down with Vlad to discuss life after retiring from the military in 2001 at age 38 and spending the next decade as a paramilitary contractor in Afghanistan, Iran, and other conflict zones. Comstock details the dangers of operating with small teams, recruiting and leading indigenous fighters, Taliban infiltration, ambush risks, and the loss of fellow Delta operators during the Global War on Terrorism. He also explains how political restrictions around detentions and interrogations changed the mission on the ground, arguing that bureaucracy put American lives at risk.

Reflecting on war, Comstock agrees with Elon Musk’s widely shared view that wars are often driven by older leaders sending young men to kill one another. He offers a critical but personal perspective on the military, politicians, civilians, and the realities faced by soldiers and contractors in modern warfare.

Charleston White sits down with Vlad for a raw discussion about prison culture, racial dynamics, and sexual violence behind bars. Reacting to Ramon “Mundo” Mendoza’s accounts from Mexican Mafia life, White recalls hearing older inmates say, “in every white boy, there’s a little white girl waiting to come out,” while describing how white inmates were targeted in Texas, Alabama, and other Southern prisons. The conversation also examines how attitudes toward prison assault shifted by the late ’80s and ’90s, plus differences on the East Coast, Washington, D.C., and in facilities seen on MSNBC’s *Lockup*. Vlad and White revisit *American Me*, Edward James Olmos, the controversial Mexican Mafia rape scene, and Mendoza’s claims about Joe Morgan, his brother Angel, Kern County, and the Black Guerrilla Family.
